claims.text: The initially solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles have a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Surface-mediated atomic processes govern the onset and progression of the phase transition in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Increasing temperature increases atomic diffusion in the nanoparticles.
Thermally activated diffusion promotes selective surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements.
Selective segregation produces surface compositional gradients in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Surface segregation and pronounced surface-energy effects locally lower the melting temperature.
The locally reduced melting temperature initiates a melting front at the nanoparticle surface.
The surface-initiated melting front propagates inward.
Nanoparticles with enhanced surface segregation will begin surface melting earlier than nanoparticles retaining a uniform composition.
Surface-segregated nanoparticles will undergo the phase transition at a lower temperature than the homogeneous baseline.
Surface effects dominate the thermal response of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles below approximately 50 nm.
The proposed behavior may differ in larger particles or under oxidizing atmospheres.
A mild annealing pretreatment can enhance surface segregation.
A passivation coating can suppress surface segregation.

Similar melting-onset temperatures and melting progression in segregation-enhanced and segregation-suppressed groups would falsify the proposed governing role of surface segregation and surface diffusion.
